Hi, this week I've began working on and contributing to the DeepMind formal-conjectures repo and opened a couple PRs today! Is there a preferred Zulip stream or some norm for asking for reviews on those PRs? Also, aside from the style guidelines in the repo README are there more guidelines or templates for what commit messages or PR messages should look like, or what comments in the Lean files should look like and how they should be organized? I've been trying to copy recent commits and PRs I've seen so far.

Links:
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3431
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3467
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3438 - this one I just formalized the first part or sub-question of the Erdos problem, still need to add the rest

Just quickly glancing at those PRs, they look pretty good as is! There isn't really a Zulip channel for asking for reviews, but the maintainers do seem a bit backlogged at the moment with reviews, so probably just give them time to get around to your PRs.

For the Erdos Problems, there's this README for naming conventions.

Thank you! And thanks to @Moritz Firsching for all his help with the reviews!!

Also I had another question in case anyone here can answer quickly since it's probably a common one: I formalized Fuglede's conjecture in a PR but this is closely related to my area of research so I'm familiar with many more open problems in this area, which I've bullet pointed here: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3497#issuecomment-4027712115

I was wondering how I should deal with this: they all share some common machinery (lemmas/definitions of things like "spectral") which should probably go in some common place in the repo? Also, should I create issues for each one or put some of them together?

Hello all,

I am new to this Zulip channel.

I have posted issue and made a corresponding pull request (PR) for my conjecture on
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures

"A Bounded Capacity Generalization of the Classic n-Queens Problem".

I want to excuse myself for changing both the issue and the PR all to often.
Recall that I am new to Google Deepmind and this formal conjectures channel.

I think that my conjecture falls into the category of
"simple question with difficult answer"
conjectures.

I joined this channel in order to receive more feedback.

I am a retired mathematician, interested in new technologies.

I sincerely hope that some members of this channel are interested in my issue and PR as well.
Hey Luke, thanks for the PR! I haven’t had a look yet, but simple problems with hard answers are very much in scope generally speaking:)

Hi! I am a new contributor and would like to ask about the appropriate next step.

I noticed that Written on the Wall II Graph Conjecture 316 is currently tagged @[category research open].

I have produced a Lean 4 proof of the formalized statement:

  • Github: GitHub repository
  • Lean4web: Open the proof in Lean4Web

It compiles without sorry or admit, both against the Formal Conjectures definitions and in the current Lean4Web environment. The formalization and write-up were prepared with AI assistance, as disclosed in the README.

Should I now open a GitHub issue proposing that the conjecture be changed from research open to research solved?
Hey there! Opening a PR sounds good (note that you can also link your formal proof using the formal_proof attribute!

Hi!

I'm a newbie to Lean (and Zulip, and PRs for that matter :) ), but took a type theory class a while ago.

I put together a formalization of detecting cliques using (unbounded fan-in) NAND gate circuits. Obviously, in general, this is getting at the P?=NP question. The motivation was to see if AIs could obtain any weak bounds, even for tiny circuits, and, like, input graphs with 8 vertices. That already seems quite hard; but trying simpler problems is often a good idea...

The formalization
(using Antigravity a fair bit) is in a separate repository. This is mostly because I wasn't sure how doable this would be, or if it was interesting to people. Note that it only formalizes the problem; it doesn't even prove a naive upper bound...

If it sounds possibly useful, and close enough to correct, I'm happy to open a PR relative to the Formal Conjectures repo, and add it somewhere. If people have comments on this, please let me know.

Josh Burdick
